Chapter 3: Recognizing and Disarming Shame
Shame is such a quiet force, isn’t it? Most of the time, it’s just there in the background, quietly shaping our choices and keeping our true selves under wraps.
Think about it: shame isn’t like guilt. Guilt is what you feel when you’ve done something wrong—shame, though, clings to who you are. It’s that nagging voice that says, “You’re not enough.” And so, you hide the parts of yourself you’re scared others won’t accept.
The real power of shame? It thrives on secrecy. Most of us don’t talk about it, not even with our closest friends or family. The more we keep it hidden, the stronger it gets.
Let me share a story that really brings this to life. Picture a young professional, eager to make a good impression at work. She makes a costly mistake, and instead of owning up to it, she tries to cover it up, hoping no one will catch on. The anxiety grows, and soon she feels completely isolated. When the truth finally surfaces, she’s bracing herself for the worst. But her manager responds with empathy—sharing a similar mistake from years earlier. The relief is almost instant. In that moment, shame loses its tight grip.
Here’s something to pay attention to: naming shame is the first step in taking away its power. When you actually say what you’re feeling—whether it’s fear of failing, not fitting in, or being exposed—you start to realize you’re not alone. Everyone faces moments of doubt and insecurity. The real difference is in how we handle them.
There’s another story I want to share. A mother, struggling with postpartum depression, kept her feelings bottled up for months. She worried that admitting her struggles would make her a bad parent. But when she finally opened up to a friend, she found out she wasn’t alone at all. That friend listened—really listened—without any judgment. Together, they found support and resources. And that’s when it became clear: sharing shame, instead of hiding it, is what leads to healing.
Building resilience to shame doesn’t mean you’ll never feel it again. It means learning to recognize when it shows up, and choosing how you’ll respond. That often starts with reaching out to someone you trust—someone who listens, without trying to jump in and fix everything or brush your feelings aside. It also means pushing back against that harsh inner critic, the one that tries to convince you your mistakes are proof you’re not worthy.
Shame shows up everywhere, even at work. When people are afraid of being embarrassed or punished, they stop sharing new ideas. They keep quiet when things aren’t going well, and that’s how innovation gets stifled. But when leaders are willing to admit their own vulnerabilities, they create a space where everyone feels safer to speak up. And in families, talking openly about shame helps kids learn how to bounce back from setbacks and criticism.
Over time, it becomes clear: shame grows in silence. But as soon as you bring it into the open, it starts to lose its hold. By recognizing it and naming it, you take back control. You connect with others. And you realize that everyone struggles sometimes—real belonging isn’t about being perfect, it’s about being seen for who you truly are.
